source_read: PMC HTML, PMC11916924 (author manuscript; Ann Epidemiol 2025;102:8–22, online 21 Dec 2024), read in full in the reader's own browser tab (title confirmed): abstract, introduction, methods, results 1–2.3.2 with Tables 1–3, discussion, conclusion, references (refs 33, 36, 37 checked: all Ruhm CJ). Figure 1 (PRISMA diagram) not viewed. All findings of the included studies are second-hand (the review's own summaries).

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the review; the claim correctly narrows the review's cross-study presentation of the 20–35% range to its actual basis.
claims.note: The part attributed to this review checks: its national range (21–35% for any opioid, 20–35% for heroin or synthetic opioids) cites only refs 33, 36 and 37, all by Ruhm, all imputation analyses of the same NVSS multiple-cause files over overlapping years (1999–2012, 2008–2014, 1999–2015); the abstract presents it as a cross-study finding and the Discussion as consistent with two state studies (Horon; Quast); the review assessed no study's risk of bias. The review also supports the dependence on place and period (unspecified share about 25% in 2008–2010, 15–20% in 2014–2016, 8% in 2018, about 6% in 2020; 0% to 63.8% across states in 2008) and reports linkage studies the claim does not use (Kentucky 2013–2014: a quarter of certificates named no drug although 89% of those deaths had toxicology; Florida 2003–2017: medical examiners' records held 8,633 more opioid deaths than national data, 34%; Marion County, Indiana 2011–2016: 87% of unspecified deaths opioid-positive). Part not supported as worded: the closing sentence that no study read here measured how often stimulants are missed. The review's Table 2 reports, second-hand, a Florida comparison (Quast, 2020) in which national multiple-cause counts fell well short of the state medical examiners' counts for benzodiazepines and opioids, less for amphetamines, with a large cocaine gap late in the period: an unlinked count comparison, but a measurement of stimulant deaths missing from national data. The review's own Discussion still calls for studies of stimulant misclassification. Suggested wording: 'apart from one Florida count comparison reported second-hand (Quast, 2020, in Gutkind et al., 2025)'.

anchors.locator: Results › 2.2.1, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results
anchors.extracted: Four national studies of NVSS multiple-cause data; corrected opioid-related counts (all intents) 21–35% higher for any opioid and 20–35% higher for heroin or synthetic opioids, depending on period, from three multiple-imputation studies, refs 33, 36, 37 (Ruhm 2017, 2016, 2018). Fourth study (Buchanich, ref 35): about 72% of unspecified unintentional deaths 1999–2015 estimated opioid-related under an equal-proportion assumption. Abstract states the 20–35% national underestimate as a finding across studies; Discussion calls it consistent with state studies (refs 40, 41).

anchors.locator: Table 2, Ruhm C 2018 row; Methods › 2. Review and analysis
anchors.extracted: Ruhm 2018 (NVSS 1999–2015; year-specific probit models fitted to deaths naming at least one drug, used to predict opioid involvement where no drug was named): 23.1% unspecified (26% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015); corrected counts 21–35% (all opioids) and 20–35% (heroin/synthetic) above reported. The review did no risk-of-bias assessment of included studies.

anchors.locator: Results › 2. Misclassification of Cause of Death, 1st paragraph; Results › 2.1, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Share of overdose deaths without a specific drug: about 25% in 2008–2010, 15–20% in 2014–2016, 8% in 2018, about 6% by 2020. In 2008, from 0% (District of Columbia) to 63.8% (Louisiana); South Carolina fell from 39.8% (2008) to 6.0% (2014).

Florida local overdose records: 8,633 more opioid-related deaths than NVSS, 34% of the NVSS count, 2003–2017. Kentucky 2013–2014: a quarter of overdose certificates unspecified although 89% of those deaths had postmortem toxicology; linkage added 2% as heroin-related. Kentucky 2015: 88% with toxicology; linkage showed 4.7% (heroin) and 6% (fentanyl) more. Marion County, Indiana 2011–2016: 87% of unspecified deaths opioid-positive on toxicology.

Florida 2003–2017, national multiple-cause counts against Florida Medical Examiners Commission counts by drug: national counts substantially smaller, with sizeable gaps for benzodiazepines and opioids and smaller ones for amphetamines; by the end of the period the cocaine gap was large while the methadone gap narrowed.

Authors call for future evaluation of misclassification in polysubstance and stimulant deaths. They also state, citing expert guidance, that drug screens can label a death drug-involved when drugs were used but did not contribute, and that incomplete scene notes can miss drug involvement (assertions, not measurements).

claims.overstatement: No overstatement: the claim reports Denham's odds ratios as odds; the review's own text restates the 2018 odds ratio as a fourfold likelihood (risk language), which the claim avoids.
claims.note: The second-hand sentence checks: three studies (Warner 2013, Denham 2022, Tote 2019) found fewer unspecified certificates with medical examiners than with coroners; Denham's odds ratios for an unclassified overdose death in coroner counties were 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (national multiple-cause data). Points for the editor: (1) per the review's table, Denham adjusted for individual, county and state-level covariates rather than comparing counties within the same state, and Tote used state and county random effects, so 'in the same states' in the claim's opening sentence rests mainly on Lundberg (manner of death) rather than on these drug-specificity studies; (2) the review's Table 1 says Warner (2008–2010) found the undetermined-manner share varied by state but not by investigation system, a second-hand qualifier on the Lundberg association; (3) Denham also found lower odds where the coroner or medical examiner is a pathologist, where coroners must be trained and in centralized systems, and a larger 2014–2018 fall in unspecified deaths in medical-examiner counties (72% against 43%); (4) the review's suggestion that elected coroners hesitate to certify opioid deaths is speculation without data.

anchors.extracted: Three studies (refs 17, 32, 34) found lower percentages of unspecified overdose deaths in states and counties with medical examiners than with coroners; centralized medical-examiner states lower than decentralized; 2014 to 2018 the fall in unspecified deaths was 72% in medical-examiner counties against 43% in coroner counties and the gap widened. The text renders the 2018 odds ratio as 'four times more likely'.

anchors.locator: Table 1, Denham et al. 2022 row (Key Findings 1–5)
anchors.extracted: National multiple-cause data, 2014 and 2018, all intents: unclassified 19.3% (2014) and 8% (2018); coroner system associated with higher odds of an unclassified overdose death, OR 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (multivariable logistic regression with individual, county and state covariates and month fixed effects); lower odds where the coroner or medical examiner is a pathologist, violent deaths are investigated, coroners must be trained, or the system is centralized.

National 2010–2016: 20.3% of overdose deaths lacked drug specification, 24.4% (2010) to 14.6% (2016); missing specification less likely in urban counties and medical-examiner (versus coroner) counties, in a multilevel model with state and county random effects.
National 2008–2010: the undetermined-manner share varied by state but not by investigation system; the share of certificates specifying a drug varied by state and by system.

Authors attribute the system differences to training and qualifications (unspecified deaths fell where coroners had to be trained or be pathologists) and suggest elected coroners may be reluctant to certify an opioid overdose because of consequences for families; no data are given for the latter.

claims.overstatement: Minor: the review's table says heroin, morphine and codeine were 'involved' in the Allegheny deaths; the claim's 'deaths attributed to morphine' is slightly stronger than that wording, though the review's text does describe the Allegheny certificates as under-reporting heroin.
claims.note: Allegheny County and New York City numbers check against the review's Table 3 (Mertz; Gill) and its text (74 added heroin deaths = 245 − 171, 66% of 112; 84 of 118 = 71%, heroin deaths up 17%). Points for the editor: (1) in New York, 61 of the 84 rested on toxicology (diacetylmorphine, 6-acetylmorphine, or codeine measured against morphine) and the rest on other evidence; Allegheny's criteria mixed history, scene items, track marks and 6-acetylmorphine: presence rather than cause, as the claim says of the other reviews; (2) the falls in morphine and codeine deaths (91 + 29 = 120) exceed the heroin rise (74), unexplained in the review (overlapping categories likely); (3) the review reports more second-hand evidence the claim omits: SUDORS 2018–2019 (38 states and DC), where 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths had only morphine on the certificate and reclassification raised the heroin share from 80.2% to 93.3%; Kentucky 2015, 4.7% of overdose deaths heroin-positive with no drug named plus 2.3% heroin-positive without heroin listed; Kentucky 2013–2014, 44 more deaths (2%) flagged by the morphine-to-codeine ratio, which the review's table calls highly predictive (relevant to the claim's remark that the position paper cites no test of the ratio rule); San Francisco 2006–2012, +21% in the text but 20 more on 152 (+13%) in Table 3. The multi-state SUDORS finding would strengthen a claim that now speaks of three places.
